lesson.title: First Sentences Gym
lesson.subtitle: Fourteen words you already own are enough for six real German sentences

hook.title: You Already Have Enough Words
hook.content: Vocabulary lists lie to beginners. They imply you need five hundred words before a sentence is legal. You already know lernen, kommen, gehen, singen, schwimmen, finden, bringen — plus Haus, Glas, Brot, and friends. German sentences need only three parts: a doer, an action in position 2, and everything else. Six sentences from today, and every one is built from words English handed you.

footnotes.title: Old English Did It Too
footnotes.content: Old English main clauses also tended to set the verb second ('Hwæt! We Gar-Dena...' — the verb 'we have' comes right after the first phrase). Verb-second is not a German quirk; it is the ancestral English habit that modern English lost.

pattern.title: Subject — Verb — Everything Else
pattern.content: The rule: the conjugated verb is glued to position 2, no matter what. Ich lerne Deutsch. Wir lernen Deutsch. Notice the verb barely changes: ich lernt? No — ich lernt is wrong; ich lernt sounds like a parrot, ich lernt... ich lerne ends in -e for 'I', and wir lernt? wir lernen — the full -en returns for 'we'. So: ich lerne, wir lernen; ich schwimme, wir schwimmen; ich finde, wir finden. Two people, two endings, one stem. German has not even asked you to memorize anything yet.

footnotes.title: ich ↔ I
footnotes.content: Even the word 'ich' is your old possession: English 'I' and German 'ich' descend from the same Proto-Germanic *ek. The vowel wandered for a thousand years — the word never changed owner.

exercises.explanation: Stem 'lern-' takes -e for ich: ich lerne. The -st is the du-ending — not this person.

exercises.prompt: Match each German sentence with its English meaning. Then recall earlier vocabulary in the short phrases:
exercises.target_answer: Wir schwimmen, Ich finde das Glas, Wir singen, Ich komme, Ich lerne Deutsch, Ich finde die Wurst, Gold im Sand, der Ring
exercises.meaning: We swim; I find the glass; We sing; I come; I learn German; I find the sausage; gold in the sand; the ring
exercises.explanation: Subject + verb in position 2: with wir the verb keeps its full dictionary -en. Deutsch, Wurst — zero-shift words slot straight in.

exercises.meaning: Wir finden den Kuchen = We find the cake
exercises.explanation: Stem 'find-' + the full -en for wir = finden. Der Kuchen is the cake — collect the masculine flag with the word.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is a correctly built German statement?
exercises.meaning: I learn German — verb glued to position 2
exercises.explanation: The conjugated verb stays in position 2: subject first, then verb, then everything else.

vocab_hints.note: ancient twin of English 'and' — both from the same Proto-Germanic word

exercises.explanation: Two nouns joined by 'und'; bringen holds position 2 of its half — das Bier needs no translation, only a capital letter.

summary.outcome: Build simple subject-verb sentences with ich and wir forms of seven cognate verbs.

use_example.german: Wir lernen Deutsch und wir singen.
use_example.english: We learn German and we sing.

summary.takeaway: Verb in position 2, ich takes -e, wir takes -en — the sentence writes itself from words you already own.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: brighten, shorten, deepen — English has its own living -en verbs, and they unlock a whole shelf of German ones.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from First Sentences Gym (We bring bread and beer):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Wir bringen Brot und Bier" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of First Sentences Gym without relying on short-term echo.

lernen.context_translation: I am learning German with Brücke.
lernen.etymology_derivation: Shared root *liznōną (to follow a track/learn) + infinitive -en.

singen.etymology_derivation: Initial S voiced to [z] before vowels.

finden.context_translation: I cannot find it / I find it not.
finden.etymology_derivation: Stem find + infinitive -en (German keeps pure short [ɪ] vowel).

bringen.etymology_derivation: Shared ancient Germanic mixed verb (bring/brought ↔ bringen/gebracht).

haus.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hūsą — an exact twin of English house, down to the diphthong. [wiktionary]

brot.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *braudą — originally "the fermented/risen thing", kin to the verb brew (German brauen). Bread is "the brewed thing". [wiktionary]

deutsch.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *þiudiskaz, of the people, built on *þeudō, people; the very same word as English Dutch, with Latin theodiscus and Teutonic sharing the root. [wiktionary]

bier.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *beuzą. Medial ie produces pure tense monophthong [iː].

kuchen.context_translation: Would you like a piece of cake?
kuchen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kōkô; Wiktionary names only Dutch koek — see Apfelkuchen. [wiktionary]

wurst.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *wursti; English wurst is only a later borrowing from German — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

segeln.context_phrase: Im Sommer segeln wir auf dem See.
segeln.context_translation: In summer we sail on the lake.
segeln.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *seglōn, the verb of Segel (sail) - the page lists English sail as a direct cognate. [wiktionary]

großstadt.context_phrase: Die Großstadt ist laut, aber spannend.
großstadt.context_translation: The big city is loud but exciting.
großstadt.etymology_derivation: groß + Stadt — the big city; groß is the twin of great (t → ß). [wiktionary]
